staff.title: WHO RUNS THE GAME?
staff.directorText: Coordinates operations and staff. In tournaments, oversees structure, timing and organization; matters requiring a higher decision may be referred to the director under house procedures.
staff.floorText: Supervises tables and resolves questions, disputes and irregularities. Establishes what happened and applies house rules. If a problem arises, request the floor and preserve cards and chips until instructed.
staff.dealerText: Runs the hand: deals cards, tracks action order and manages bets and pots. Point out errors promptly; when interpretation or a dispute is involved, the dealer calls the floor.
decisions.title: POKER IS A GAME OF CONTINUOUS DECISIONS
decisions.intro: Every action or new card changes the situation. Pokerinno helps you go through the cycle again.
decisions.observeText: Your cards, position, pot and previous action: what do you know now?
decisions.optionsText: Fold, check, call, bet or raise? Check which actions are available and what each costs.
decisions.chooseText: Choose with a reason: seek value, control the pot, bluff or avoid further risk.
decisions.followText: Did an opponent respond or a new card appear? Update your assessment before the next choice.
decisions.reviewText: Understand your reasoning. Winning does not prove the choice was good; losing does not prove it was bad.
decisions.exampleText: On the flop, someone bets and action reaches you. What is the first step?
decisions.answerText: Observe before clicking. Compare the call amount with the pot, consider your potential to improve and what the opponent may represent. Calling keeps you in the hand but costs chips; folding avoids more spending but gives up the pot; raising invests more and changes the pressure. Without cards, stacks and full context, there is no single answer.

math.description: Understand the purpose of each calculation, when to use it, how to work it out and how to apply it.
math.host.title: MATH HELPS YOU MAKE DECISIONS
math.host.text: Start with the decision you need to make. Understand the calculation’s purpose, check its inputs and follow an example before using it at the table.
math.host.quote: Understand the calculation to make better decisions.
math.note.title: UNDERSTAND BEFORE CALCULATING
math.note.text: Each item includes its name, purpose and objective, timing, calculation and example. Card references use 52-card Texas Hold’em; C(n,k) means choosing k cards from n without regard to order. Simple call and bluff calculations specify when there are no further bets or rake.
math.items.out.name: OUT
math.items.out.purpose: Identifies one specific card that improves your hand. The objective is to check whether it can also make your hand a winner rather than counting every improvement.
math.items.out.when: On the flop or turn, when assessing a draw before calling or betting.
math.items.out.how: List the cards that complete the desired hand. Count each physical card once and discount cards that still leave you behind the opposing range.
math.items.out.example: With A♥ Q♥ on a 9♥ 6♥ 2♣ flop, 3♥ completes a flush: it is a candidate out. Its quality depends on the opponent’s possible hands.
math.items.outs.name: OUTS
math.items.outs.purpose: Counts the distinct cards that can complete your hand. This total is the starting point for estimating your improvement probability.
math.items.outs.when: On the flop and turn before converting a draw into a percentage.
math.items.outs.how: Count clean outs without double-counting cards shared by two draws. A flush draw normally has 13 cards of the suit − 4 known cards = 9 outs.
math.items.outs.example: A♥ Q♥ on 9♥ 6♥ 2♣ leaves 9 unknown hearts. With both straight and flush draws, count the union of the outs rather than adding them blindly.
math.items.odds.name: ODDS
math.items.odds.purpose: Expresses a probability as a ratio of failures to successes. It helps compare your chance of hitting with the price offered by the pot.
math.items.odds.when: When comparing draw probabilities with pot odds or converting a percentage into a ratio.
math.items.odds.how: For odds against the event, use (1 − p) ÷ p, where p is a decimal. Read the result as failures to 1 success.
math.items.odds.example: A 20% chance gives (1 − 0.20) ÷ 0.20 = 4. The odds against are 4:1, or four misses for each hit on average.
math.items.probability.name: PROBABILITY
math.items.probability.purpose: Measures the chance of an event. The goal is to distinguish common from rare events and quantify opportunities without treating an estimate as a certainty.
math.items.probability.when: Before the flop for starting-hand frequencies, on the flop and turn for draws, and when reviewing results.
math.items.probability.how: For equally likely outcomes: probability = favorable outcomes ÷ possible outcomes × 100. Otherwise, add the probabilities of the favorable outcomes.
math.items.probability.example: There are 6 AA combinations among 1,326 starting hands: 6 ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ 0.45%. This is the chance of receiving AA, not the chance of winning.
math.items.combo.name: COMBO
math.items.combo.purpose: Represents one specific card combination. It helps count possible hands in an opposing range and identify blockers.
math.items.combo.when: When building preflop ranges and reviewing value hands and bluffs after accounting for your cards and the board.
math.items.combo.how: List available two-card hands without considering their order. Remove known cards first; A♠ K♥ and K♥ A♠ are the same combo.
math.items.combo.example: AA has 6 combos. If you hold A♠, only C(3,2) = 3 AA combos remain for the opponent.
math.items.combinatorics.name: COMBINATORICS
math.items.combinatorics.purpose: Counts sets of cards without duplication. The aim is to find the denominator and favorable outcomes for hand and board probabilities.
math.items.combinatorics.when: When studying ranges, starting-hand frequencies, flops and exact equity calculations.
math.items.combinatorics.how: C(n,k) = n! ÷ [k! × (n − k)!]. For two cards: C(n,2) = n × (n − 1) ÷ 2. The ! symbol means multiplying the integers from 1 through that number.
math.items.combinatorics.example: Hold’em hands: C(52,2) = 52 × 51 ÷ 2 = 1,326. With your two cards known, there are C(50,3) = 19,600 possible flops.
math.items.equity.name: EQUITY
math.items.equity.purpose: Measures your average share of the pot if the remaining cards are dealt and the hand reaches showdown. It provides a basis for comparing price and expected value.
math.items.equity.when: When facing an all-in, estimating your hand against a range and studying decisions. With future betting, equity alone does not determine EV.
math.items.equity.how: Heads-up: equity = (wins + ties ÷ 2) ÷ outcomes × 100. Against a range, weight each matchup by its frequency; for multiway ties, use the actual share of the pot.
math.items.equity.example: In 100 equally likely outcomes, you win 40, tie 10 and lose 50: (40 + 10 ÷ 2) ÷ 100 × 100 = 45% equity.
math.items.fold-equity.name: FOLD EQUITY
math.items.fold-equity.purpose: Accounts for the value gained when your bet makes the opponent fold. The objective is to evaluate the contribution of folds to EV alongside your equity when called.
math.items.fold-equity.when: When assessing a bluff or semi-bluff and estimating how often the opposing range folds.
math.items.fold-equity.how: For a heads-up model with no further bets or rake: bet EV = F × P + (1 − F) × [q × (P + 2B) − B]. F is fold probability, P the pot before your bet, B your bet and q your equity when called.
math.items.fold-equity.example: Assume P = 100, B = 50, F = 40% and q = 20%: EV = 0.40 × 100 + 0.60 × (0.20 × 200 − 50) = 34 chips. Folds contribute 40 chips to that sum.
math.items.ev.name: EXPECTED VALUE — EV
math.items.ev.purpose: Compares decisions by their expected average gain or loss. The goal is to choose the highest-EV action from the current decision point without confusing one hand’s result with decision quality.
math.items.ev.when: Before calling, betting or folding, and during hand review. Chips already invested are sunk costs; evaluate the new investments.
math.items.ev.how: EV = sum of probability × net result for each outcome. For a call with no further bets or rake: EV = q × final pot − call, with q including your share of ties.
math.items.ev.example: Pot 100, opponent bets 50, call 50 and equity 30%: final pot 200; EV = 0.30 × 200 − 50 = +10 chips. In this model, folding is worth 0 from the decision point.
math.items.break-even.name: BREAK-EVEN
math.items.break-even.purpose: Finds the condition where an action has zero EV. The objective is to determine how often you must win or make the opponent fold to cover the new investment.
math.items.break-even.when: Before a call or bluff, as a threshold against which to compare your estimate.
math.items.break-even.how: Set EV to zero and solve for the probability. For a call with no further bets or rake: minimum q = call ÷ final pot. For a pure one-bet bluff: minimum folds = bet ÷ (pot + bet).
math.items.break-even.example: Call 50 to contest a final pot of 200: q = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%. EV = 0.25 × 200 − 50 = 0. More than 25% is positive in this model.
math.items.risk-reward.name: RISK / REWARD
math.items.risk-reward.purpose: Compares the amount at risk with the possible net gain. It helps measure an action’s price and minimum success frequency.
math.items.risk-reward.when: When comparing call and fold or choosing a bluff size in a simple model.
math.items.risk-reward.how: Risk = new investment; reward = chips gained in addition to the return of that investment. For win-or-lose outcomes without ties, minimum success = risk ÷ (risk + reward).
math.items.risk-reward.example: The available pot before your call is 150 and calling costs 50. You risk 50 to gain 150 net: reward/risk = 3:1; break-even = 50 ÷ 200 = 25%.
math.items.frequency.name: FREQUENCY
math.items.frequency.purpose: Measures the proportion of times an action or event occurs. The goal is to compare observed behavior, range composition and assumptions used in calculations.
math.items.frequency.when: During session review and when estimating folds, calls or bluffs. Count only opportunities where that action was possible.
math.items.frequency.how: Frequency = occurrences ÷ opportunities × 100. A small sample can fluctuate substantially and does not by itself establish the true strategy.
math.items.frequency.example: In an example with 25 opportunities to face a bet, the player folds 15 times: 15 ÷ 25 × 100 = 60% folds.
math.items.pot-odds.name: POT ODDS
math.items.pot-odds.purpose: Measures the price of contesting the pot. The aim is to find the minimum share of the final pot your call must recover to have nonnegative EV.
math.items.pot-odds.when: When facing a bet. Direct comparison with equity applies with no further bets or rake; otherwise, consider how the equity will be realized.
math.items.pot-odds.how: Minimum equity = call ÷ (available pot including the opponent’s bet + your call) × 100. If P is the pot before the opponent’s bet B: call B ÷ (P + 2B) × 100.
math.items.pot-odds.example: Pot 100, opponent bets 50 and you call 50: 50 ÷ (100 + 50 + 50) × 100 = 25%. With 30% realizable equity, EV = 0.30 × 200 − 50 = +10.
math.items.implied-odds.name: IMPLIED ODDS
math.items.implied-odds.purpose: Considers additional chips you may win on later streets after completing a winning hand. The aim is to assess whether that gain can offset a call without sufficient direct odds.
math.items.implied-odds.when: On the flop and turn, particularly with stacks that allow future payoffs. Estimate whether the opponent will actually pay when your draw completes.
math.items.implied-odds.how: In a model where every hit wins and misses incur no further investment: required future net gain = call ÷ hit probability − (available pot before the call + call). Future payoffs are estimates.
math.items.implied-odds.example: Available pot 150, call 50 and hit probability 20%: 50 ÷ 0.20 − 200 = 50 additional chips when you hit to break even. Check whether that payoff is plausible given stacks and the opposing range.
math.items.reverse-implied-odds.name: REVERSE IMPLIED ODDS
math.items.reverse-implied-odds.purpose: Considers additional losses when you improve but still hold the second-best hand. The goal is to avoid overvaluing low draws and dominated hands.
math.items.reverse-implied-odds.when: When calling with a low draw, a weak-kicker pair or other hands that may improve and still lose, particularly with deep stacks.
math.items.reverse-implied-odds.how: There is no universal percentage. Separate future winning and losing outcomes; expected additional value = sum of probability × net result. Discount outs that do not make a winning hand.
math.items.reverse-implied-odds.example: 8♠ 7♠ on K♠ 2♠ Q♦ 4♠ makes a flush but loses to A♠ J♠. In a hypothetical future-investment model, a 40% chance of gaining 100 and a 60% chance of losing 80 give 0.40 × 100 − 0.60 × 80 = −8.
math.items.spr.name: SPR — STACK-TO-POT RATIO
math.items.spr.purpose: Compares the remaining effective stack with the pot. The aim is to measure room for future betting and plan commitment to the hand.
math.items.spr.when: Primarily at the start of the flop and when planning later streets, before new bets.
math.items.spr.how: SPR = remaining effective stack ÷ pot at the start of the street. Use the same unit for both. The number alone does not determine which hands should go all-in.
math.items.spr.example: A 20 BB pot and 60 BB effective stack give SPR = 60 ÷ 20 = 3. The effective stack is three times the pot.
math.items.effective-stack.name: EFFECTIVE STACK
math.items.effective-stack.purpose: Identifies how much two players can contest against each other. The aim is to correctly limit risk, implied odds and SPR calculations.
math.items.effective-stack.when: Before an all-in, when planning bets and assessing future payoffs. In multiway pots, evaluate each opponent and the side pots.
math.items.effective-stack.how: Between two players, effective stack = the smaller remaining stack. Compare stacks in the same unit and at the same moment in the hand.
math.items.effective-stack.example: You have 100 BB and the opponent 60 BB: effective stack = minimum(100,60) = 60 BB. Your other 40 BB cannot be won by that opponent in this contest.
math.items.call-percentage.name: CALL AS A PERCENTAGE OF THE POT
math.items.call-percentage.purpose: Describes the call size relative to the pot already available. The aim is to express the price without confusing it with the minimum equity from pot odds.
math.items.call-percentage.when: When comparing call prices and checking which denominator a calculation uses.
math.items.call-percentage.how: Relative price = call ÷ available pot before the call × 100. For minimum equity, the denominator changes: call ÷ (available pot + call) × 100.
math.items.call-percentage.example: Available pot 150 and call 50: the payment is 50 ÷ 150 ≈ 33.33% of the current pot. Minimum equity is 50 ÷ 200 = 25%, not 33.33%.
math.items.mdf.name: MDF — MINIMUM DEFENSE FREQUENCY
math.items.mdf.purpose: Provides a reference for range defense against a pure one-bet bluff. The goal is to understand how much folding would make that bluff automatically profitable in the model.
math.items.mdf.when: When studying defense, particularly on the river. It includes calls and raises, not an obligation to call every hand; texture, ranges and exploitation can change the correct defense.
math.items.mdf.how: For the first bet B into pot P in a simple zero-equity bluff model: MDF = P ÷ (P + B) × 100. Do not apply this formula directly to the cost of a raise.
math.items.mdf.example: Pot 100 and bet 50: MDF = 100 ÷ 150 × 100 ≈ 66.67% of the range. With 90 equally weighted combos, the reference is to defend 60, split between calls and raises.
math.items.alpha.name: BLUFF ALPHA — REQUIRED FOLDS
math.items.alpha.purpose: Finds the minimum fold frequency for a pure bluff to break even. The aim is to compare the bet’s risk with the folds you expect.
math.items.alpha.when: Before a first zero-equity bluff bet with no future action, when a call always loses the bet.
math.items.alpha.how: Alpha = bet B ÷ (pot P + bet B) × 100. Bluff EV = F × P − (1 − F) × B. The model excludes rake; raises and semi-bluffs require modeling costs and equity.
math.items.alpha.example: Betting 50 into 100: alpha = 50 ÷ 150 ≈ 33.33%. Assuming 40% folds, EV = 0.40 × 100 − 0.60 × 50 = +10 chips.
math.items.rule-two.name: RULE OF TWO
math.items.rule-two.purpose: Quickly estimates the chance of hitting an out with one card to come. The aim is to provide a mental reference before comparing the price.
math.items.rule-two.when: From flop to turn or turn to river. It considers only the next card.
math.items.rule-two.how: Approximate percentage = clean outs × 2. This is a shortcut; for precision, divide outs by the unknown cards.
math.items.rule-two.example: 9 outs on the turn: 9 × 2 ≈ 18%. The exact value is 9 ÷ 46 × 100 ≈ 19.57%, with only your two cards and the board known.
math.items.rule-four.name: RULE OF FOUR
math.items.rule-four.purpose: Estimates the chance of hitting by the river from the flop. The aim is to approximate a two-card probability without mistaking it for the next-card probability.
math.items.rule-four.when: On the flop when you can see both turn and river for the cost already considered, as in an all-in. A flop call may require another payment on the turn.
math.items.rule-four.how: Approximate percentage = clean outs × 4. Accuracy worsens with many outs; use the exact two-card formula in those cases.
math.items.rule-four.example: 9 outs on the flop: 9 × 4 ≈ 36%. Exact by the river: [1 − (38 ÷ 47) × (37 ÷ 46)] × 100 ≈ 34.97%. This measures hitting an out, not guaranteed victory.
math.items.one-card.name: EXACT ONE-CARD PROBABILITY
math.items.one-card.purpose: Calculates the chance that the next card belongs to your set of outs. The aim is to provide a more precise reference than mental shortcuts.
math.items.one-card.when: On the flop for the turn or on the turn for the river, revising your outs after each card.
math.items.one-card.how: Probability = outs ÷ unknown cards × 100. In Hold’em with only your hand and the board known, there are 47 on the flop and 46 on the turn. Additional exposed cards change the count.
math.items.one-card.example: 9 outs: flop → turn = 9 ÷ 47 ≈ 19.15%; turn → river = 9 ÷ 46 ≈ 19.57%. The denominator falls because another card becomes known.
math.items.receive-aa.name: BEING DEALT AA
math.items.receive-aa.purpose: Shows how often you are dealt AA. The aim is to calibrate expectations and understand starting-hand composition without confusing frequency with strength.
math.items.receive-aa.when: During preflop study and volume review. Do not use this frequency as equity against an opponent.
math.items.receive-aa.how: Count favorable combos: {ways}. Divide by C(52,2) = 1,326 starting hands and multiply by 100. The average interval is 1,326 ÷ favorable combos.
math.items.receive-aa.example: One hand in this group is A♠ A♥. {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%: on average, one occurrence every {every} hands. This is not a guaranteed interval.
math.items.receive-pair.name: BEING DEALT ANY POCKET PAIR
math.items.receive-pair.purpose: Shows how often you are dealt any pocket pair. The aim is to calibrate expectations and understand starting-hand composition without confusing frequency with strength.
math.items.receive-pair.when: During preflop study and volume review. Do not use this frequency as equity against an opponent.
math.items.receive-pair.how: Count favorable combos: {ways}. Divide by C(52,2) = 1,326 starting hands and multiply by 100. The average interval is 1,326 ÷ favorable combos.
math.items.receive-pair.example: One hand in this group is 7♠ 7♥. {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%: on average, one occurrence every {every} hands. This is not a guaranteed interval.
math.items.receive-ak.name: BEING DEALT AK — SUITED OR OFFSUIT
math.items.receive-ak.purpose: Shows how often you are dealt AK of any suits. The aim is to calibrate expectations and understand starting-hand composition without confusing frequency with strength.
math.items.receive-ak.when: During preflop study and volume review. Do not use this frequency as equity against an opponent.
math.items.receive-ak.how: Count favorable combos: {ways}. Divide by C(52,2) = 1,326 starting hands and multiply by 100. The average interval is 1,326 ÷ favorable combos.
math.items.receive-ak.example: One hand in this group is A♠ K♦. {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%: on average, one occurrence every {every} hands. This is not a guaranteed interval.
math.items.receive-aks.name: BEING DEALT AK SUITED
math.items.receive-aks.purpose: Shows how often you are dealt AK of the same suit. The aim is to calibrate expectations and understand starting-hand composition without confusing frequency with strength.
math.items.receive-aks.when: During preflop study and volume review. Do not use this frequency as equity against an opponent.
math.items.receive-aks.how: Count favorable combos: {ways}. Divide by C(52,2) = 1,326 starting hands and multiply by 100. The average interval is 1,326 ÷ favorable combos.
math.items.receive-aks.example: One hand in this group is A♠ K♠. {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%: on average, one occurrence every {every} hands. This is not a guaranteed interval.
math.items.receive-suited.name: BEING DEALT TWO SUITED CARDS
math.items.receive-suited.purpose: Shows how often you are dealt two cards of the same suit. The aim is to calibrate expectations and understand starting-hand composition without confusing frequency with strength.
math.items.receive-suited.when: During preflop study and volume review. Do not use this frequency as equity against an opponent.
math.items.receive-suited.how: Count favorable combos: {ways}. Divide by C(52,2) = 1,326 starting hands and multiply by 100. The average interval is 1,326 ÷ favorable combos.
math.items.receive-suited.example: One hand in this group is 9♥ 6♥. {favorable} ÷ 1,326 × 100 ≈ {percent}%: on average, one occurrence every {every} hands. This is not a guaranteed interval.
math.items.flop-flush.name: SUITED → FLOPPING A FLUSH
math.items.flop-flush.purpose: Measures the chance of three cards of your suit on the flop. The goal is to quantify how rare a made flush is; being suited does not guarantee a strong hand.
math.items.flop-flush.when: Preflop when assessing suited-hand expectations, and when studying possible flop outcomes.
math.items.flop-flush.how: With your two cards known and no other exposed cards: {formula} × 100. Count favorable boards and divide by the total; for 1 − formulas, first count boards that miss.
math.items.flop-flush.example: With A♠ K♠, one example flop is Q♠ 7♠ 2♠. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.items.flop-flush-draw.name: SUITED → FLOPPING A FLUSH DRAW
math.items.flop-flush-draw.purpose: Measures the chance of exactly two cards of your suit on the flop. The goal is to recognize how often postflop starts with a flush draw rather than a made hand.
math.items.flop-flush-draw.when: Preflop when studying suited hands, and on the flop to recognize four cards of one suit across your hand and the board.
math.items.flop-flush-draw.how: With your two cards known and no other exposed cards: {formula} × 100. Count favorable boards and divide by the total; for 1 − formulas, first count boards that miss.
math.items.flop-flush-draw.example: A♠ K♠ on Q♠ 7♠ 2♦ has a flush draw and normally 9 remaining spades. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.items.flop-straight.name: CONNECTORS → FLOPPING A STRAIGHT
math.items.flop-straight.purpose: Measures the chance of a connector such as 7-6 making a straight with the three flop cards. The aim is to calibrate expectations rather than equate connectedness with a made straight.
math.items.flop-straight.when: Preflop when studying connectors. Edge hands such as A-2 or K-Q have fewer possible straights than 7-6.
math.items.flop-straight.how: With your two cards known and no other exposed cards: {formula} × 100. Count favorable boards and divide by the total; for 1 − formulas, first count boards that miss.
math.items.flop-straight.example: For 7♠ 6♦, the flop rank groups are 3-4-5, 4-5-8, 5-8-9 and 8-9-T. Each group has 4³ suit combinations; 5♥ 4♣ 3♣ is an example. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.items.flop-set.name: POCKET PAIR → HITTING ITS RANK ON THE FLOP
math.items.flop-set.purpose: Measures the chance of at least one of the two remaining cards of your pair appearing on the flop. The goal is to understand set-mining frequency and compare cost with potential future winnings.
math.items.flop-set.when: Preflop before calling with a pocket pair to hit a set. Hit probability alone does not decide the call; stacks and future payoffs matter.
math.items.flop-set.how: With your two cards known and no other exposed cards: {formula} × 100. Count favorable boards and divide by the total; for 1 − formulas, first count boards that miss.
math.items.flop-set.example: With 7♠ 7♥, a 7♦ K♣ 2♠ flop makes a set. The calculation also includes flops with both remaining sevens, making quads. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.items.flop-rank.name: UNPAIRED HAND → HITTING AT LEAST ONE RANK
math.items.flop-rank.purpose: Measures the chance that the flop contains at least one card of either of your ranks. The goal is to understand why two high cards often miss both pairs.
math.items.flop-rank.when: Preflop when calibrating expectations for hands such as AK or AQ. After the flop, assess the actual board rather than the previous probability.
math.items.flop-rank.how: With your two cards known and no other exposed cards: {formula} × 100. Count favorable boards and divide by the total; for 1 − formulas, first count boards that miss.
math.items.flop-rank.example: With A♠ K♦, 3 aces and 3 kings remain. A♥ 9♣ 3♦ hits one rank; the count also includes two-pair, trips and full-house results. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.items.flop-two-pair.name: UNPAIRED HAND → TWO PAIR USING BOTH HOLE CARDS
math.items.flop-two-pair.purpose: Measures the chance of making exactly two pair with both of your ranks on the flop. The goal is to quantify this rare improvement without including full houses.
math.items.flop-two-pair.when: During preflop study of unpaired hands and review of possible flop outcomes.
math.items.flop-two-pair.how: With your two cards known and no other exposed cards: {formula} × 100. Count favorable boards and divide by the total; for 1 − formulas, first count boards that miss.
math.items.flop-two-pair.example: A♠ K♦ on A♥ K♣ 3♦: choose 1 of the 3 aces, 1 of the 3 kings and 1 of the 44 cards of other ranks. There are 396 favorable flops. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.items.suited-river.name: SUITED → MAKING A FLUSH BY THE RIVER
math.items.suited-river.purpose: Measures the chance of at least three cards of your suit appearing on the complete board. The goal is to separate flush frequency from the overall strength or equity of a suited hand.
math.items.suited-river.when: During preflop study, assuming all five board cards are dealt. Do not use this probability as the price for calling just one street.
math.items.suited-river.how: With your two cards known and no other exposed cards: {formula} × 100. Count favorable boards and divide by the total; for 1 − formulas, first count boards that miss.
math.items.suited-river.example: A♠ K♠ on Q♠ 7♦ 2♠ 5♥ 9♠ makes a flush. Boards with 3, 4 or 5 spades are counted; making a flush does not guarantee winning. Result: {favorable} ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}%.
math.items.flush-draw.name: FLUSH DRAW — 9 OUTS
math.items.flush-draw.purpose: Counts the 9 remaining cards of the suit after four are known. The goal is to estimate flush completion while discounting cards that do not make a winning hand.
math.items.flush-draw.when: On the flop before calling or betting; recalculate on the turn. The by-river probability assumes seeing two cards for the cost considered and outs that remain valid.
math.items.flush-draw.how: With {outs} outs: flop → turn = {outs} ÷ 47 × 100; flop → river = [1 − ({missOne} ÷ 47) × ({missTwo} ÷ 46)] × 100. From turn to river, use {outs} ÷ 46 × 100.
math.items.flush-draw.example: A♠ Q♠ on 9♠ 6♠ 2♦: 13 − 4 = 9 remaining spades. With {outs} clean outs: next card ≈ {next}%; by the river ≈ {river}%; on the turn with one card left ≈ {turn}%. Completion does not guarantee victory.
math.items.oesd.name: OESD — OPEN-ENDED STRAIGHT DRAW — 8 OUTS
math.items.oesd.purpose: Counts the two ranks that complete an open-ended straight. The goal is to estimate completion without counting cards that leave an inferior straight or allow an opponent’s flush.
math.items.oesd.when: On the flop before calling or betting; recalculate on the turn. The by-river probability assumes seeing two cards for the cost considered and outs that remain valid.
math.items.oesd.how: With {outs} outs: flop → turn = {outs} ÷ 47 × 100; flop → river = [1 − ({missOne} ÷ 47) × ({missTwo} ÷ 46)] × 100. From turn to river, use {outs} ÷ 46 × 100.
math.items.oesd.example: J♠ T♦ on 9♥ 8♣ 2♠: any 7 or Q completes the straight; 4 + 4 = 8 candidates. With {outs} clean outs: next card ≈ {next}%; by the river ≈ {river}%; on the turn with one card left ≈ {turn}%. Completion does not guarantee victory.
math.items.gutshot.name: GUTSHOT — INSIDE STRAIGHT DRAW — 4 OUTS
math.items.gutshot.purpose: Counts the four cards of the rank that fills the straight’s gap. The goal is to assess a less frequent draw against a suitable price or future payoff.
math.items.gutshot.when: On the flop before calling or betting; recalculate on the turn. The by-river probability assumes seeing two cards for the cost considered and outs that remain valid.
math.items.gutshot.how: With {outs} outs: flop → turn = {outs} ÷ 47 × 100; flop → river = [1 − ({missOne} ÷ 47) × ({missTwo} ÷ 46)] × 100. From turn to river, use {outs} ÷ 46 × 100.
math.items.gutshot.example: J♠ T♦ on 8♥ 7♣ 2♠: only a 9 completes 7-8-9-T-J, so there are 4 candidates. With {outs} clean outs: next card ≈ {next}%; by the river ≈ {river}%; on the turn with one card left ≈ {turn}%. Completion does not guarantee victory.
math.items.pair-two-outs.name: POCKET PAIR WITHOUT A SET — 2 OUTS
math.items.pair-two-outs.purpose: Measures the chance of one of the two remaining cards of your pair appearing after missing a set on the flop. The aim is to quantify how difficult improvement is rather than justify calls solely on hope.
math.items.pair-two-outs.when: On the flop before calling or betting; recalculate on the turn. The by-river probability assumes seeing two cards for the cost considered and outs that remain valid.
math.items.pair-two-outs.how: With {outs} outs: flop → turn = {outs} ÷ 47 × 100; flop → river = [1 − ({missOne} ÷ 47) × ({missTwo} ÷ 46)] × 100. From turn to river, use {outs} ÷ 46 × 100.
math.items.pair-two-outs.example: 7♠ 7♥ on K♦ 9♣ 2♠: the candidates are 7♦ and 7♣. With {outs} clean outs: next card ≈ {next}%; by the river ≈ {river}%; on the turn with one card left ≈ {turn}%. Completion does not guarantee victory.
math.items.overcards.name: TWO OVERCARDS — UP TO 6 OUTS
math.items.overcards.purpose: Estimates the chance of pairing one of your two ranks above the board. The goal is to recognize that up to 6 cards improve the hand, but not all beat the opposing range.
math.items.overcards.when: On the flop before calling or betting; recalculate on the turn. The by-river probability assumes seeing two cards for the cost considered and outs that remain valid.
math.items.overcards.how: With {outs} outs: flop → turn = {outs} ÷ 47 × 100; flop → river = [1 − ({missOne} ÷ 47) × ({missTwo} ÷ 46)] × 100. From turn to river, use {outs} ÷ 46 × 100.
math.items.overcards.example: A♠ K♦ on Q♥ 7♣ 2♠: 3 aces + 3 kings = up to 6 candidates. Against a set or two pair, a single pair may still lose. With {outs} clean outs: next card ≈ {next}%; by the river ≈ {river}%; on the turn with one card left ≈ {turn}%. Completion does not guarantee victory.
math.items.combo-draw.name: COMBO DRAW — 15 CLEAN OUTS
math.items.combo-draw.purpose: Counts the union of a flush draw and an open-ended straight draw. The goal is to measure the chance of completing at least one draw without double-counting shared outs.
math.items.combo-draw.when: On the flop before calling or betting; recalculate on the turn. The by-river probability assumes seeing two cards for the cost considered and outs that remain valid.
math.items.combo-draw.how: With {outs} outs: flop → turn = {outs} ÷ 47 × 100; flop → river = [1 − ({missOne} ÷ 47) × ({missTwo} ÷ 46)] × 100. From turn to river, use {outs} ÷ 46 × 100.
math.items.combo-draw.example: J♠ T♠ on 9♠ 8♦ 2♠: 9 spades + 8 Q/7 cards − Q♠ and 7♠ already counted = 15 candidates, if all are clean. With {outs} clean outs: next card ≈ {next}%; by the river ≈ {river}%; on the turn with one card left ≈ {turn}%. Completion does not guarantee victory.
math.items.aa-random.name: AA × RANDOM HAND
math.items.aa-random.purpose: Shows the average advantage of AA against a uniformly random opposing hand. The aim is to calibrate variance; this reference does not automatically represent a real all-in range.
math.items.aa-random.when: When studying equity and variance. At the table, replace the random hand with the range the opponent can actually hold.
math.items.aa-random.how: Fix your two aces. For each of the C(50,2) = 1,225 opposing hands, count wins and shares of ties over possible boards and take the uniform average. The reference is approximately 85%, with differences for particular opposing hands.
math.items.aa-random.example: Using 85% as an approximate reference in a final pot of 200: 0.85 × 200 = 170 chips as the average pot share. The result of any individual hand remains uncertain.
math.items.aa-kk.name: AA × KK
math.items.aa-kk.purpose: Quantifies the first hand’s average pot share against the second. The aim is to understand advantage, domination and variance for a matchup with specific cards and suits.
math.items.aa-kk.when: Before a preflop all-in or when studying known heads-up hands. An opposing range requires weighting multiple matchups; different suits change equity.
math.items.aa-kk.how: Fix all four cards. Enumerate C(48,5) = {total} boards, compare each player’s best five-card hand and count wins W and ties T. Equity = (W + T ÷ 2) ÷ {total} × 100.
math.items.aa-kk.example: {hero} against {villain}: ({wins} + {ties} ÷ 2) ÷ {total} × 100 ≈ {percent}% for the first hand. Ties count as half a pot share; the complement belongs to the second hand.

math.items.bet-quarter.name: BET OF 1/4 TIMES THE POT
math.items.bet-quarter.purpose: Finds the equity threshold for calling this bet size heads-up. The aim is to compare your expected share of the pot with the call’s cost.
math.items.bet-quarter.when: When facing this bet size and considering call or fold. The direct reference assumes no rake or further bets and that your equity is realized.
math.items.bet-quarter.how: Use pot P before the opponent’s bet and the amount B you must call: minimum equity = B ÷ (P + 2B) × 100. Your call also goes into the final pot.
math.items.bet-quarter.example: Pot 100, opponent bets {bet} and you call {bet}: final pot {finalPot}; {bet} ÷ {finalPot} × 100 ≈ {percent}%. At the exact threshold EV = 0; above it, calling has positive EV in this model.
